en: The Perfection of Wisdom in Seven Hundred Lines, also known as the Mañjuśrī Chapter.
Om! Homage to the Blessed Noble Perfection of Wisdom.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a great saṅgha of bhikṣus consisting of a full thousand arhat bhikṣus,
and together with ten hundred thousand bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, all of whom were fully armored with the great armor and were irreversible from unexcelled [enlightenment].
of perfect enlightenment—
namely, Mañjuśrī the Youthful and Maitreya;
With unimpeded eloquence and with unwavering persistence, he was accompanied by these and ten hundred thousand other bodhisattvas, headed by these [two].
Then, at the time when the sun had risen, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta emerged from his own monastery and proceeded to where the Tathāgata’s monastery was.
Having arrived, he stood at the outer gate of the monastery in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Tathāgata.
Then the Venerable Śāradvatīputra also emerged from his own monastery and proceeded to where the Tathāgata’s monastery was, in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One.
Then the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
and the venerable Mahākāśyapa—
The venerable Mahākātyāyana, the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila,
and other great śrāvakas also emerged from their respective monasteries and approached the monastery where the Blessed One was staying.
Having approached, they stood to one side.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that the assembly of great disciples had arrived in great numbers, emerged from his own dwelling and sat down on a seat prepared to one side outside the gate.

Having sat down, the Blessed One, though already knowing [the answer], addressed the venerable Śāradvatīputra: "Śāradvatīputra, why have you come so early this morning and stood at the door of the Tathāgata’s dwelling?"

When this had been said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta was the very first to stand at the door of the Tathāgata’s dwelling; only afterwards did we, desiring to see the Blessed One, arrive."

Then the Blessed One, although he already knew, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Is it true, Mañjuśrī, that you were indeed the very first to stand at the door of the Tathāgata’s dwelling in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Tathāgata?"
When this had been said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Blessed One as follows: “So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
I arrived first, having departed from my own abode and approached the abode of the Tathāgata.”
Having approached, he stood to one side to behold, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One.
Why was that?
Because, Blessed One, I am never satiated by beholding, paying homage to, and attending upon the Tathāgata.
Moreover, Blessed One, whenever I approach the Tathāgata for the purpose of seeing him, paying homage, and attending upon him,
it is for the sake of all sentient beings.
If, Blessed One...
The Tathāgata is to be seen, to be venerated, and to be attended upon; he is to be seen in this way,
and he is to be venerated in this way.
He should be attended upon in this way: as I see him, as I pay homage to him, and as I attend upon him;
in this manner, the Tathāgata is seen, honored, and attended upon.
"And I, Blessed One, behold the Tathāgata for the sake of all sentient beings.
The Blessed One said, "Mañjuśrī, how is the Tathāgata to be seen, and even how is he to be served?
Mañjuśrī replied, "I behold the Tathāgata in the form of suchness (tathatā), in the form of non-conceptuality, through the yoga of non-apprehension."
In this way, I perceive the Tathāgata through the aspect of non-arising, up to perceiving the Tathāgata through the aspect of non-existence;
yet suchness does not come into being.
Thus do I see the Tathāgata:
suchness neither comes into being nor passes away; thus do I see the Tathāgata.
Suchness does not abide in a location, nor does it abide in a specific place;
thus do I perceive the Tathāgata.
Suchness is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Thus do I see the Tathāgata.
Suchness is neither characterized by duality nor characterized by non-duality;
thus do I see the Tathāgata.
Suchness is neither defiled nor purified;
thus do I perceive the Tathāgata.
Suchness neither arises nor ceases.
"In this way I see the Tathāgata;
in this way the Tathāgata becomes seen, saluted, and attended.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, seeing in this way, what do you see?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Seeing thus, O Blessed One, I see nothing at all.
Seeing in this way, I see neither the arising nor the cessation of any dharma whatsoever."

Then the Venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, you are a doer of what is difficult, you who thus behold the Tathāgata and thus attend upon him, and for whom great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings has arisen."
And yet, you have no perception of a sentient being whatsoever, nor any attachment to a sentient being;
you have set out for the parinirvāṇa of all sentient beings,
and no attachment to a sentient being arises in you at all.
"And for the sake of all sentient beings, you have donned the armor;
and that [armor] is donned by means of non-apprehension, up to and including the yoga of non-existence.
When this was said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta spoke thus to the venerable Śāradvatīputra: "It is so, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it is just as you say."
This armor has been donned for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa;
yet, I have no apprehension of a sentient being, nor any attachment to a sentient being.
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, this armor is not donned in such a way as to think: "How might I cause the realm of sentient beings to diminish or to increase?"

Venerable Śāradvatīputra, if by way of conceptualization there were Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in each individual Buddha-field, and if each Tathāgata were to remain for aeons as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, teaching the Dharma day and night, and if with each single teaching of the Dharma they were to discipline as many sentient beings as have been disciplined by all those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who are themselves as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges;
If each and every Tathāgata were to discipline that many sentient beings through a single teaching of the Dharma,
even by doing so, no decrease or increase in the realm of sentient beings would be perceived.
For what reason?
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, because sentient beings are isolated and because sentient beings do not exist, neither decrease nor increase is perceived in the realm of sentient beings.

When this had been said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, if— due to the solitude of sentient beings and the non-existence of sentient beings— not even increase or decrease is perceived in the realm of sentient beings, then for whom will you now teach the Dharma after having fully awakened to enlightenment?"
When this had been said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the venerable Śāradvatīputra: "Venerable Śāradvatīputra, since beings are ultimately non-apprehensible, who here will attain perfect awakening,
or for whom will the Dharma be taught?"
For what reason?
Because, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, there is the absolute non-apprehension of all phenomena.
Then the Blessed One said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, since all phenomena are ultimately non-apprehendable, why now would you designate even a 'sentient being'?
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, if someone were to ask: 'How many sentient beings are there?'"
"What would you say to him?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Lord, if I were asked that, I would say: 'As many as are the qualities of a Buddha (buddhadharma).
Lord, if he were to ask again, 'What is the measure of the realm of sentient beings (sattvadhātu)?'"
O Blessed One, if I were asked this, I would say: "The extent of the Buddha's domain is such as it is."
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, if someone were to ask you again, 'To what is the realm of sentient beings included?', what would you say to him?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Blessed One, if I were asked that, I would say: 'It is included in the non-arising and the inconceivability.'"
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, if someone were to ask you again, 'Upon what is the realm of sentient beings established? what would you say to him?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Blessed One, if asked that, I would say to him: 'The realm of sentient beings is established upon that upon which the realm of non-arising is established.'"
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, at the time when you cultivate the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), where do you cultivate that perfection of wisdom as being established?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Blessed One, at the time when I cultivate the perfection of wisdom,"
At that time, being non-abiding, I cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, for you who are non-abiding, what is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Blessed One, that very thing which is non-abiding anywhere is itself the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom."
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, at the time when you cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), which of your roots of merit (kuśalamūla) at that time undergoes increase or decrease?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Blessed One, at that time, no root of merit of mine whatsoever undergoes either increase or decrease."
He does not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for whomsoever there is either an increase or a decrease of any dharma.
O Blessed One, that should not be known as the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom which stands for the sake of the increase or the decrease of any dharma.
That, Blessed One, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom which neither abandons the dharmas of ordinary persons nor appropriates the dharmas of a Buddha.
For what reason?
For it is thus, Blessed One: the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom does not arise through the apprehension of any dharma such that one might abandon or take up that dharma.
That, Blessed One, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom which neither approaches the faults of saṃsāra nor the qualities of nirvāṇa.
For what reason?
For in this way, Blessed One, I do not even perceive saṃsāra itself,
let alone the faults of saṃsāra;
I do not even apprehend nirvāṇa itself.
How much more so, Blessed One, will I behold the qualities of nirvāṇa?
That cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, Blessed One, is that which involves neither the taking up, nor the grasping, nor the departure from any dharma whatsoever.
That cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, Blessed One, is that in which neither the decrease nor the increase of any dharma whatsoever is perceived.
For what reason?
Because, O Blessed One, non-arising neither decreases nor increases. Such, O Blessed One, is cultivation.
That is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom which does not produce or cease any dharma whatsoever.
O Blessed One, that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom which effects neither the diminution nor the fulfillment of any dharma.
O Blessed One, that which is such a cultivation is itself the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, that cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is that which does not seek after inconceivable phenomena, nor partial phenomena.
Moreover, O Blessed One, that which is sought, that by which one seeks, and that wherein one seeks— all that does not exist.
In this way, O Blessed One, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom:
these phenomena are superior, these phenomena are inferior—
yet one does not apprehend those phenomena for which there might be superiority or inferiority.
In this way, a son of good family who is devoted to the practice of the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend any phenomena.
Blessed One, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom does not conceptualize any phenomenon as either superior or inferior.
For what reason?
For indeed, Blessed One, there is nothing superior or inferior in non-arising, nor in suchness, nor in the limit of reality.
To whatever extent there is anything among all phenomena— whether superior or inferior—
it is thus, O Blessed One, that the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is cultivated.
When this had been said, the Blessed One addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, are not the Buddha-dharmas supreme?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Blessed One, the Buddha-dharmas are supreme because they are ungraspable.
[The Blessed One asked: "Then, Blessed One, have all dharmas been realized by the Tathāgata as empty?"
The Blessed One said, “It is so, Mañjuśrī; all phenomena are empty, as the Tathāgata has perfectly awakened to them.
Mañjuśrī asked, “In that case, Blessed One, is superiority or inferiority perceived within emptiness?
The Blessed One said, “Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
"It is so, Mañjuśrī, just as you say.
But, Mañjuśrī, are the Buddha-dharmas not supreme?
Mañjuśrī replied, "It is so, Blessed One; the Buddha-dharmas are supreme."
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, not even an atom of a dharma exists or is apprehended in them;
those are not the unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas.

Furthermore, Blessed One, that cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is not conducive to the fulfillment of the qualities of a Buddha, nor is it conducive to the abandonment of the qualities of ordinary persons;
it does not discipline the qualities of a Buddha, nor does it sustain them.
In this way, Blessed One, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Blessed One, that cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is to be viewed as that which does not think of any dharma and does not cognize any dharma.
The Blessed One said, "Mañjuśrī, do you not think of the Buddha-dharmas?
Mañjuśrī replied, "No, Blessed One."
"I might contemplate the Buddha-dharmas, O Blessed One,

if I were to perceive the full accomplishment of the Buddha-dharmas. But, Blessed One, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom does not appear through the conceptualization of any dharma, such as 'these are the dharmas of ordinary persons'."
"These are the dharmas of the śrāvakas, these are the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, and these are the dharmas of the samyaksaṃbuddhas.
For what reason is that?

O Blessed One, a son of good family who is devoted to the yoga of cultivating the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend that very dharma for which he might designate these dharmas— whether they be the dharmas of an ordinary person or the dharmas of one in training.
Whether he were to point out the qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*) or the qualities of a perfectly awakened Buddha (*samyaksaṃbuddhadharma*),
I do not perceive those qualities as existing in an ultimate sense.
In this way, Blessed One, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

For a son of good family who is devoted to the application of the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, Blessed One, it does not occur to him: "This is the realm of desire; this is the realm of form."
This is the formless realm, up to and including this realm of cessation.
For what reason is that?
For indeed, Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that perceives the nature of cessation.
In this way, Blessed One, cultivation should be understood as the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Blessed One, this cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is that which does not bring about benefit or harm to any dharma whatsoever.
For indeed, Blessed One, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is neither the nurturer of the Buddha-dharmas nor the destroyer of the dharmas of ordinary persons.
O Blessed One, this indeed is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom: that which is neither the cessation of the dharmas of ordinary persons,
nor the cessation of the dharmas of a Buddha,
nor the attainment of the dharmas of a Buddha.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you teach such a profound Dharma as this.
Mañjuśrī, you have established this seal for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and for those Śrāvakas who are conceited."
And for the sake of the true awakening of those who grasp at objective apprehension and those belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle—

Mañjuśrī, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who, having heard this profound teaching on the perfection of wisdom, do not tremble, are not terrified, and do not fall into terror, will not have attended upon only a single Buddha, nor will they have planted roots of merit under only a single Buddha.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, those who, having heard this profound teaching on the perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it and will not tremble, not be terrified, and not fall into terror, will indeed have planted roots of merit under thousands of Buddhas.

When this had been said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Blessed One as follows: “Blessed One, it occurs to me to provide a further exposition of the perfection of wisdom. “Let it occur to you, Mañjuśrī,” the Blessed One said to him.
Mañjuśrī said: "O Blessed One, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) which does not perceive the stability of any dharma, nor its instability.
For what reason?
Because all dharmas are non-abiding, it does not perceive them."
This alone, O Blessed One, should be understood as the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom,
which does not stand for the sake of taking any dharma as an object of apprehension.
Why is that?
For thus, Blessed One, all dharmas are without objective support;
such, Blessed One, is the cultivation that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Blessed One, that cultivation of the perfection of wisdom should be viewed as one in which even the qualities of a Buddha do not appear before one, let alone the qualities of a Pratyekabuddha;
nor do the qualities of a Śrāvaka appear before one, so what need is there to mention the qualities of an ordinary person?
Furthermore, Blessed One, that cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is such that,

by relying upon it, one does not fall into conceptual construction even regarding the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha, thinking, "The qualities of a Buddha are inconceivable. Blessed One, this cultivation of the perfection of wisdom by bodhisattva mahāsattvas should be regarded as being for the sake of non-conceptualization toward all phenomena.
Furthermore, Blessed One, that cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is that cultivation by means of which one perceives all phenomena as Buddha-phenomena;
one perceives all phenomena as inconceivable phenomena through the manner of non-perception.

"Blessed One, those sons of good family and daughters of good family who, having heard this exposition of the perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it and will not be afraid, will not be terrified, and will not fall into terror, will have attended upon many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas."
Furthermore, Blessed One, that cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is that in which one does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as being either afflicted or purified.
Such, Blessed One, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
And this, Blessed One, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom which does not create any distinction among ordinary persons.
It does not produce differentiation among śrāvakas, nor differentiation among pratyekabuddhas, up to and including differentiation among perfectly enlightened buddhas.
This, O Blessed One, is that cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
(SaptaŚ, Vaidya 345) Then the Blessed One addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: “Mañjuśrī, how many Tathāgatas have you attended upon?

Mañjuśrī replied: “Blessed One, as many as the mental states and mental factors (*cittacaitasika*) of an illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*) have ceased, so many Tathāgatas, Blessed One, have I attended upon.”
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, are you not established in the Buddha-dharmas?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Furthermore, Blessed One, is any such dharma apprehended that is not established in the Buddha-dharmas?
The Blessed One said: "But for whom, Mañjuśrī, do these Buddha-dharmas belong?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Blessed One, even for you, these so-called 'buddha-qualities' do not exist and are not apprehended;
how much less, then, will they belong to others?
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, have you attained non-attachment?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Lord, since I am already entirely without attachment, why should I further attain non-attachment?
The Blessed One asked: "Mañjuśrī, are you then seated upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)?"
Mañjuśrī said: "The Blessed One himself has not yet sat upon the seat of awakening; how then shall I sit there, taking the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) as my standard?
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, of what is 'the limit of reality' a designation?"
Mañjuśrī said, “O Blessed One, ‘the limit of reality’ (bhūtakoṭi) is a designation for the view of a self-identity (satkāya).
The Blessed One asked, “With what intention, Mañjuśrī, do you speak thus?
Mañjuśrī replied, “O Blessed One, this body does not exist; it is not a real self-identity.”
It does not transmigrate, nor does it transmigrate away;
therefore, this body is a non-existent body (asatkāya).

Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who, having heard this teaching on the perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it and will not be afraid, will not be terrified, and will not fall into terror, will certainly be destined for awakening."

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who, having heard this teaching on the perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it, and will not be afraid, will not be terrified, and will not fall into terror, will be near to awakening."
For what reason? Because,
Blessed One, this very awakening consists in the thorough realization of these phenomena.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, having heard this teaching on the perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it, and will not be afraid, will not be terrified, and will not fall into terror— they should be regarded as Buddhas themselves."
For what reason?
"Buddha" is, in the ultimate sense, a designation for non-arising.

Then, indeed, the sister Nirālambā said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, having heard this teaching on the perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it, will not long for the qualities of ordinary persons, the qualities of śrāvakas, the qualities of pratyekabuddhas, or the qualities of perfectly enlightened buddhas."
They will not be afraid, they will not be terrified, and they will not fall into terror.
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, all phenomena are without objective support, as they do not exist.
Therefore, no objective referent exists for them.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāradvatīputra: "It is so, Śāradvatīputra, it is so.
Those sons of good family and daughters of good family who, having heard this exposition of the perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it, shall become fixed for enlightenment."
They do not tremble, they do not fear, and they will not fall into terror;
Śāradvatīputra, you should know that those sons of good family and daughters of good family are established on the stage of non-retrogression.
Those who, having heard this exposition of the perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it, and will not tremble, will not be terrified, will not fall into terror,
and will receive it upon their heads.

Śāradvatīputra, those who, having heard this exposition of the perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it, they will become supreme masters of giving, great masters of giving, and distinguished masters of giving. Śāradvatīputra, they will be endowed with ethical discipline; they will possess supreme ethical discipline and attain the path of the most distinguished qualities of ethical discipline.
They will not tremble, they will not be terrified, and they will not fall into fear;
those, Śāradvatīputra, are endowed with supreme patience and supreme vigor.
They will be endowed with supreme meditative concentrations and with supreme, incomparable wisdom.
Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, Śāradvatīputra, will eventually be endowed with the omniscient knowledge that is possessed of the excellence of all modes.
Those who, having heard this exposition of the perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it, and will not be afraid, will not be terrified, and will not fall into terror.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, [the Buddha] said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, perceiving what purpose do you desire to awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Blessed One, if I were to establish myself in enlightenment, it would be in that way that I would desire to awaken."
“I do not seek awakening, Blessed One.
Why is that?
This very Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta is awakening itself.”
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you point out such profound and profound matters as these.
For you have performed services under previous Victors and have long practiced the holy life in non-apprehension."
Mañjuśrī said: "O Blessed One, the Dharma would indeed have been attained by me if I were one who courses in non-apprehension."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, do you see this perfection of my disciples?
Mañjuśrī replied: "I see it, Blessed One.
The Blessed One asked: "How do you see it?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Blessed One, I see in such a way that I do not see ordinary persons at all,
nor do I see those in training, nor do I see those beyond training."
I do not see,
nor do I not see;
thus do I see.
That I see neither many nor few; that I see neither those who are disciplined, nor...
Nor do I see those who are undisciplined.

Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, since you view those belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas in this way, how then do you view those belonging to the vehicle of the perfectly awakened ones?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Venerable Śāradvatīputra, I do not perceive any such thing as a 'bodhisattva' as a real phenomenon."

I do not perceive any such phenomenon as "one who has set out for enlightenment"; I do not perceive any such phenomenon as "one who practices for enlightenment"; I do not perceive any such phenomenon as "one who fully awakens."
"In this way, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, I see those who belong to the vehicle of the perfectly awakened ones.
Śāradvatīputra said: "But how, Mañjuśrī, do you see the Tathāgata?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Let it be, Venerable Śāradvatīputra; he is a great nāga."
Do not strike the great elephant.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta as follows: “Mañjuśrī, of what is ‘Buddha’ a designation?
Mañjuśrī replied: “Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, as for that which is called ‘self,’ of what is that a designation?”
Śāradvatīputra said: "Mañjuśrī, 'self' is a designation for non-arising.
Mañjuśrī said:
"It is so, venerable Śāradvatīputra; for whomsoever this is a designation, namely 'self'—"
"Buddha" is a designation for him.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, that which is called "Buddha" is a designation for the trackless;
for it is not possible, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, to make known by means of words that which is called "Buddha."
Even speech, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, is not easy to define as "this is speech," let alone "what is a Buddha"?
However, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, when you ask, "Of what is this a designation— 'Buddha'?"— it is as follows:
That which has not been fully realized, which has not arisen, and which will not cease;
that which is not endowed with any dharma whatsoever, and wherein there is not even a single indivisible term—
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, "Buddha" is indeed a designation for this state of being without a basis (apada).
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, one who wishes to seek the Tathāgata should seek the self.
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, "self" is a designation for the Buddha.
Just as the self absolutely does not exist and is not apprehended, so too [is the Tathāgata].
Likewise, the Buddha also does not exist at all and is not apprehended;
just as the self cannot be described by any dharma, so too the Buddha cannot be described by any dharma.
Where there is no number whatsoever,
that is called "Buddha.
Furthermore, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, it is not easy to understand that which is the designation for "self."
"It is thus, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, that it is not easy to understand what is designated by the term 'Buddha'."
Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta does not teach in such a way that beginner bodhisattvas would understand.
When this was said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the venerable Śāradvatīputra: “Venerable Śāradvatīputra, I do not teach in such a way that even accomplished arhats would understand.”
Nor do I teach in such a way that anyone would understand it.
Why is that?
Because awakening has not been understood by anyone.
Nor have they been fully awakened,
nor seen, nor heard.
It is not remembered, not produced, and not ceased.
It is not indicated, nor is it taught;
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, enlightenment is just this much.
And that awakening is neither an entity nor a non-entity.
For what reason?
Because there is nothing whatsoever to be fully awakened to by means of awakening.
Nor does awakening awaken to awakening.
Śāradvatīputra said: "Mañjuśrī, has the Blessed One not fully awakened to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)?
Mañjuśrī replied: "No, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the Blessed One has not fully awakened to the realm of phenomena. For what reason?"
For in this way, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) itself is the Blessed One.
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, if the realm of phenomena were fully awakened to by the Blessed One, then that very realm of non-arising would be subject to cessation.
Moreover, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, that very dharmadhātu is awakening.
For what reason?
Because the dharmadhātu is devoid of sentient beings.
"All phenomena are non-existent" is a designation for awakening;
it is that which is reckoned as the "dharma-realm.
For what reason is that?
For all phenomena are indeed non-dual from the perspective of the Buddha’s domain. "Non-dual," Venerable Śāradvatīputra, is a term that is non-indicative.
"Non-indicative," Venerable Śāradvatīputra, means that it is impossible to indicate this as being either conditioned or even up to unconditioned.
In that, there is no representation whatsoever; therefore, it is non-representational.
For all phenomena, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, are indeed non-representational.
For what reason?
Because there is no manifestation of any phenomena by which they could be made known while remaining therein;
even those who have set out upon the path of immediate retribution or the inconceivable path are likewise so.
And those who have issued forth from the inconceivable have issued forth from reality.
For what reason?
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, "reality" is a term for non-differentiation.
Even those who are endowed with inconceivable dharmas do not go to the heavenly realms,
nor do they go to the states of woe.
They do not go toward parinirvāṇa.
For what reason?
Because the inconceivable is not presented as something that comes or goes.
Until there is the arrival at final nirvāṇa through coming and going;
even those, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, who are established in the four root downfalls, they are established in no root.
For what reason?
Because, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, neither a root nor a summit is maintained for non-arising.
"A rootless monk"—this is a designation for a monk who is without a fixed basis.
"An arisen legal case" is a designation for the superimposition of what is excessive.
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, one who practices while superimposing what is excessive becomes worthy of offerings in the world.
For what reason?
For such is that superimposition of the superior upon the equal:
"Venerable Śāradvatīputra, a monk who possesses faith does not deserve to consume what is given in faith; Venerable Śāradvatīputra, a monk who lacks faith deserves to consume what is given in faith."
“Venerable Śāradvatīputra, a monk who is conceptualized does not deserve to enjoy what is given in faith;
a monk who is non-conceptualized, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, deserves to enjoy what is given in faith.
A monk whose guidance is unimpaired is called an Arhat with out-flows exhausted.”
Śāradvatīputra asked: "With what intention, Mañjuśrī, do you speak thus?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Equanimity is not impaired; that which is equanimity is itself the guiding principle."
It is with this in mind, venerable Śāradvatīputra, that I say: a monk who has not impaired the guiding principle is called an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted.
"One who has not crossed over fear" (or "existence"), venerable Śāradvatīputra, is a designation for an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted.
Śāradvatīputra asked: "With what intention, Mañjuśrī, do you speak thus?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Not even the slightest fears exist for him; so how could he ever overcome anything?"
With this in mind, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, I say this: "One who has not crossed over fear" is a designation for an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted.
Śāradvatīputra said: "Mañjuśrī, for whom is the term 'one who has attained the patience of the non-arisen' a designation?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Venerable Śāradvatīputra, he by whom not even the slightest dharma has been produced is called 'one who has attained the patience of the non-arisen.'"
Śāradvatīputra said: "Mañjuśrī, for whom is the expression 'an undisciplined monk' a designation?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Venerable Śāradvatīputra, 'an undisciplined monk' is a designation for an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted. For what reason?"
For it is the undisciplined who are disciplined, not the disciplined who are disciplined.
It is with this in mind, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, that I say: "an undisciplined monk" is a designation for an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted.
Śāradvatīputra said: "Mañjuśrī, for whom is this designation 'one who courses in the higher mind'?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Venerable Śāradvatīputra, 'one who courses in the higher mind' is a designation for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*.
Śāradvatīputra asked: "With what intention, Mañjuśrī, do you speak thus?"
Mañjuśrī said: "For that very reason, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, he exerts himself."
When this had been said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!
You speak just as an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted would speak.
Mañjuśrī replied: "It is even so, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, just as you say."
"I am one whose outflows are exhausted, yet I am not an Arhat.
For what reason?
Because, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, my outflows are exhausted [only] with respect to the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha."
By this method, venerable Śāradvatīputra, one whose outflows are exhausted is not yet an arhat.

Then the Blessed One said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, could there be a circumstance in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, seated at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), would be incapable of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?

Mañjuśrī replied: "Blessed One, there could indeed be such a circumstance, in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, seated at the seat of awakening, would be incapable of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
For what reason?
Because in awakening, not even the slightest phenomenon exists or is perceived;
therefore, it is called "unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening."
And that awakening is unarisen;
therein, no dharma whatsoever exists or is apprehended that could sit upon the seat of awakening.
Whether it be one who would fully awaken to enlightenment, that by which enlightenment is fully awakened to, or one who would rise from the seat of enlightenment.
In this manner, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva seated at the seat of awakening is incapable of fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, for what is 'awakening' (bodhi) a designation?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Blessed One, 'awakening' is a designation for the five deeds of immediate retribution (pañcānantarya). For what reason is that?"
For indeed, those five acts of immediate retribution are of the very nature of awakening because they are non-existent.
Therefore, this awakening has the nature of the immediate retributions; awakening is the full realization of the immediate retributions as being non-existent.
Furthermore, awakening is not the direct perception of all phenomena.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are, in an ultimate sense, beyond direct perception.
They have not been fully awakened to by anyone, nor seen, nor known.
As long as they are not known,
such is this awakening.
Moreover, Blessed One, these have been established by those possessed of overweening pride as things to be fully awakened to.
...up to being directly realized.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, do you have such a thought toward me as: 'The Tathāgata is my Tathāgata'?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One. And for what reason?"
"Blessed One, it would not occur to me that 'the Tathāgata is my Tathāgata.
Why is that?
Because suchness is exactly as suchness is."
And so it is with this Tathāgata;
for, Blessed One, suchness does not make itself known to the Tathāgata, nor does the Tathāgata make himself known to suchness.
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, from the perspective of ultimate truth, suchness is a non-entity,
and the Tathāgata is a non-entity.
Therefore, Blessed One, it does not occur to me that "the Tathāgata is my Tathāgata.
Rather, Blessed One, "Tathāgata" is merely a name.
Which Tathāgata is that one regarding whom it would occur to me that "the Tathāgata is my Tathāgata"?
The Blessed One said:
"Mañjuśrī, do you have any doubt regarding the Tathāgata?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
In this regard, O Blessed One, I have a doubt:
if there were any such thing as the accomplishment of a Tathāgata,
or the arising of a Tathāgata, or the final nirvana of a Tathāgata.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, does it not occur to you that 'the Tathāgata has arisen'?
Mañjuśrī replied: "It would occur to me, Blessed One, that 'the Tathāgata has arisen,' if there were an arising of the dharmadhātu."
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, do you not believe that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā and have entered parinirvāṇa?
Mañjuśrī replied: "But, Blessed One, are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of a single domain, namely, this inconceivable domain?
The Blessed One said: "It is so, Mañjuśrī."
"The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have a single domain, namely, an inconceivable domain.
Mañjuśrī said, "But, Blessed One, does anyone exist at present?
The Blessed One replied, "It is so, Mañjuśrī."
Mañjuśrī said: "Therefore, Blessed One, these Blessed Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, have not entered final nirvāṇa.
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, all Blessed Buddhas share a single domain, namely, the inconceivable domain."
Furthermore, inconceivability neither arises nor ceases.
Therefore, Blessed One, whether it be by the Blessed One who has attained perfect awakening,
or by those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future time—
They have indeed attained full awakening.
For what reason?
Because inconceivability is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Therefore, Blessed One, the world’s configuration is a delusion for them.
Blessed One, those who think, "The Tathāgata has arisen," up to "he will pass into parinirvāṇa," are merely proliferating the world’s configuration.

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "In that case, Mañjuśrī, you should proclaim before the Tathāgata— or before an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, or an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted— this inconceivable [nature] of the Tathāgata, which is inconceivable and beyond thought, by means of these utterances."
For what reason?
Because, having heard it, they will neither approve of it nor reject it.
"For what reason?
Because that is conceivable, inconceivable, and beyond thought.
Mañjuśrī said, "Blessed One, regarding all phenomena which are inconceivable and beyond thought, who here would either approve or reject them?"
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, just as the Tathāgata is beyond conceptualization, so too are ordinary beings beyond conceptualization.
Mañjuśrī asked: "Blessed One, are ordinary beings also, in that very same way, beyond conceptualization?"
The Blessed One said: "It is so, Mañjuśrī.
For what reason?
Because all things are inconceivable and beyond thought."
Mañjuśrī said: "For what reason, Blessed One, do you say this: 'Just as the Tathāgata is beyond thought, so too are ordinary persons beyond thought'?
Is it not the case, Blessed One, that even the state of being an ordinary person is beyond thought?"
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, all phenomena are beyond thought.
Blessed One, whoever has set out for the sake of parinirvāṇa, [they too are beyond thought].
They will dwell thus, O Blessed One.
And for what reason?
Because that very state of being free from thought is itself parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, Blessed One, there is no differentiation within the state of being beyond thought.

Furthermore, Blessed One, as for those who say, "These are the dharmas of ordinary persons; these are the dharmas of the noble ones," [they speak thus because they have not realized that all dharmas are of one taste].
They should be addressed as follows: "First, attend upon spiritual friends;
thereafter, you will come to know: 'These are the dharmas of ordinary persons; these are the dharmas of the noble ones.'"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: “Mañjuśrī, do you desire the Tathāgata to be the foremost among all sentient beings?
Mañjuśrī replied: “I would desire, O Blessed One, that the Tathāgata be the foremost among all sentient beings, provided that there were here some actual accomplishment of a sentient being.”
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, do you desire that the Tathāgata be endowed with inconceivable qualities?
Mañjuśrī replied: "I would desire, O Blessed One, that the Tathāgata be endowed with inconceivable qualities, provided that anyone could be so endowed with inconceivable qualities."
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, do you further desire this—that these śrāvakas have been disciplined by the Tathāgata?

Mañjuśrī replied: "I would desire this, Blessed One—that these śrāvakas have been disciplined by the Tathāgata—if there were anyone [capable of understanding] the discipline of the inconceivable realm."
One should go [to him].
Blessed One, the arising of a Buddha does not stand in relation to anyone through either benefit or harm.
For what reason?
For thus this realm is established;
this realm is unmixed,
namely, the inconceivable realm.
And in that realm, no diversity of śrāvakas is perceived, up to and including no diversity of ordinary persons.
The Blessed One said: "Mañjuśrī, do you not desire this—that the Tathāgata is the unsurpassed field of merit?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Because he is non-existent, O Blessed One, the Tathāgata is the field of merit; for that reason, he is the unsurpassed field of merit."
Because this is a field of merit and not a non-merit field,
it is therefore an unsurpassed field of merit.
Furthermore, Blessed One, herein no dharma whatsoever arises, nor does any perish.
In this way, it is a field of merit;
and the seed sown therein neither increases nor diminishes.
The Blessed One asked: "With what intention, Mañjuśrī, do you say that the seed sown in that field neither increases nor diminishes?"
Mañjuśrī said: "For that reason, Blessed One, that field is inconceivable; such is that field of merit."
Then, at that moment, through the power of the Buddha, a great earthquake occurred in six ways;
and the minds of sixteen thousand bhikṣus were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging,
as were seven hundred bhikṣuṇīs, three hundred upāsakas, forty thousand upāsikās, and sixty hundred billion koṭis of gods belonging to the desire realm, who became free from dust and stainless.
The Dharma-eye regarding phenomena has arisen.

Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "What, Blessed One, is the cause,
what is the condition for the manifestation of this great earthquake in the world?"

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, this Dharma discourse called 'The Exposition of the Field of Merit' was taught by previous Buddhas, Blessed Ones, in this very spot on earth. This, Ānanda, is the cause."
This is the cause for the manifestation of this great earthquake in the world.
The Perfection of Wisdom in Seven Hundred Lines is completed.
